title: Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems

concept.text: The innovation would be a fully specified deterministic algorithm that correctly solves an NP-complete problem on every input, with a proved polynomial worst-case running time and constants and exponent small enough for practical use. Boolean satisfiability, which asks whether a Boolean formula has a satisfying assignment, is a representative target. For problems in NP, a suitable proposed solution can be checked in polynomial time; the missing capability is a general, practically affordable way to find a solution or establish that none exists.

An NP-complete problem can express every problem in NP through a polynomial-time reduction. Consequently, a proved polynomial-time algorithm for any one NP-complete problem would establish P = NP. This entry requires more than that mathematical result: the algorithm must also work at useful input sizes. Cook explicitly distinguishes polynomial time from practical feasibility, discussing both an n^100 running time and prohibitively large constants. A constructive proof with such costs could settle P versus NP while leaving this practical innovation unrealized.

significance.text: A practical general algorithm would change the relationship between checking and discovering solutions across a broad class of finite problems. Cook describes roughly a thousand known NP-complete problems in his account, including problems associated with industrial scheduling and routing; the supplied SAT handbook material also discusses planning, bounded verification and combinatorial design. Under P = NP, the associated search problem for every NP problem has a polynomial-time algorithm. The revolutionary consequence would be a general guarantee for exact search, extending beyond the many instances already handled successfully by specialized solvers.

The practical transfer would remain conditional on representation and cost. Applications need suitable finite encodings and polynomial-length, polynomially verifiable witnesses; unrestricted planning and verification need not fall within NP. Exact optimization could benefit where objective thresholds can be decided through suitable NP formulations and solutions recovered with manageable overhead. Even with a practical core algorithm, encoding size, reductions and repeated search calls could make particular applications expensive. Polynomial equivalence therefore does not guarantee equally affordable performance across all application families.

Cook identifies major consequences for cryptography. A reasoned extension is that a general polynomial-time search method would remove the asymptotic hardness basis of conventional computational cryptography, including post-quantum schemes whose attacks can be formulated through efficiently checkable classical computations. Concrete compromises would still depend on the costs of the resulting encodings and algorithms. Information-theoretic secrecy would not be invalidated by faster computation alone, because its secrecy guarantee does not depend on an adversary lacking computational power.

Synthesis: this would be a foundational change in computational capability, but its downstream effects would depend on additional scientific and engineering work. Efficiently searching a formally specified space does not automatically provide a useful specification, a way to recognize every desirable outcome, an intelligent agent, a physical robot or quantum hardware. Its impact would be greatest where the desired result can already be represented and checked effectively.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is an algorithm with both universal correctness for an NP-complete decision problem and a practical polynomial worst-case bound. Success on many instances, or strong average performance on a chosen distribution, does not establish that bound. The algorithm must handle every input, including difficult unsatisfiable instances, while avoiding prohibitive constants, exponents and resource requirements. Cook's formulation asks whether every language accepted by a nondeterministic polynomial-time machine can also be accepted by a deterministic polynomial-time machine.

Known limitations on proof methods help explain the difficulty of resolving the underlying question. Cook's statement discusses relativization and the natural-proofs barrier. The latter is conditional on strong pseudorandom generators and concerns a broad class of approaches to general circuit lower bounds; it is not an unconditional barrier to every possible algorithmic argument. These results constrain particular techniques without proving that a feasible algorithm cannot exist. Algebrization was also named in the supplied research, but the supplied evidence does not substantiate its scope or relevance, so no specific conclusion about it is drawn here.

Engineering synthesis: a mathematical breakthrough would still need an implementation that preserves its useful bounds. Memory use, input representations, reduction overhead and solution recovery would need explicit accounting. A method that becomes efficient only beyond unreachable input sizes, or whose practical implementation relies on unproved shortcuts, would leave an important part of this innovation unfinished.

current_state.text: The supplied Clay Mathematics Institute overview, retrieved on 1 November 2026, labels P versus NP unsolved. That supports Clay's reported status at retrieval; the supplied materials do not document a broader literature search establishing the absence of every accepted proof. Cook's complete saved statement establishes the technical problem and the consequence of a polynomial algorithm for one NP-complete problem. Its URL contains a 2022 upload path, which does not establish when the statement was composed.

Modern SAT solving already achieves substantial practical success on industrial and other encoded problems. The 2021 second edition of the Handbook of Satisfiability documents practical complete SAT algorithms and applications in its preface and chapter abstracts. Complete solvers can correctly decide both satisfiable and unsatisfiable instances when their computation finishes; completeness does not imply a polynomial worst-case runtime or affordable resource use on every instance. The remaining gap is a general feasible worst-case method. The supplied handbook access covers its landing page, preface material and abstracts, rather than full chapters.

Cook reports that most complexity theorists believe P ≠ NP and expresses pessimism about finding a polynomial-time algorithm for an NP-complete problem. This is an attributed expert expectation, not a proof of impossibility or a forecast of when the question will be settled. Worst-case intractability has not been established. The practical algorithm described here therefore remains hypothetical and might not exist.

A related cryptographic distinction remains important when interpreting the alternatives. Brzuska and Couteau's article, published online on 4 December 2024 and assigned to a 2025 journal issue, describes deriving one-way functions from general average-case hardness as a long-standing open problem. This is a dated statement, not a verified update through November 2026. Although the supplied extraction truncates around page 51 of 70, the relevant abstract and introductory discussion were retained; access exceeded abstract-only coverage but did not include a complete extracted article.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: publish a fully specified deterministic algorithm that correctly decides Boolean satisfiability, or another NP-complete problem, on every input. Supply a machine-checked or rigorously refereed correctness proof and a worst-case time bound of C n^k, defining input length n, the computational model, the constant C and the fixed exponent k. The constants and exponent must support practical execution at declared useful sizes. Any preprocessing, auxiliary procedures or assumptions must be included in the guarantee.
completion_criteria.label: Deterministic NP-complete algorithm proved correct in practical worst-case C n^k

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical evaluation: release an implementation and public benchmark inputs, with independent reproduction across cryptographic and combinatorial families as well as industrial instances. Include satisfiable and unsatisfiable cases, declared hardware, time and memory budgets, input encodings, and reduction and solution-recovery costs. Compare performance at sizes where current complete solvers exceed those budgets. Report failures and resource limits so that practical boundaries remain visible.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction reporting resource limits where complete solvers exceed budgets

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation: the correctness and complexity proofs would establish the general mathematical claim; finite experiments would establish demonstrated breadth and practical performance on the tested families. Benchmarks cannot establish literal universality. A SAT-competition victory, a heuristic speedup or a polynomial algorithm with unusable costs would not complete this concept. A proof of P ≠ NP would settle the mathematical question in the opposite direction without supplying the requested capability.
completion_criteria.label: Generality from proofs and practical performance on tested families

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison—CSC-02, Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation: both concern major increases in computational capability, but they require distinct breakthroughs. CSC-01 seeks a practical deterministic classical algorithm with a general worst-case guarantee. Building a useful fault-tolerant quantum computer would not itself supply that algorithm, and achieving CSC-01 would not provide quantum hardware or error correction.

Roster comparison—CSC-03, Competent general machine intelligence, and CSC-08, General-purpose physical autonomy in unmodified environments: a practical NP solver could assist formally encoded planning, search and design tasks. General intelligence additionally requires useful representations, learning and judgment; physical autonomy additionally requires perception, control and reliable interaction with the world. Those capabilities do not follow automatically from an efficient solver, and neither concept is equivalent to CSC-01.

Roster comparison—CSC-04, Industrial-cost proof-carrying software, and CSC-10, Machine-checked behavioral guarantees for frontier learned models: CSC-01 could assist verification tasks that admit suitable finite encodings and polynomially verifiable witnesses. Proof-carrying software also requires usable specifications, proof production, checking and integration at industrial cost. Guarantees for learned models additionally require formal properties that meaningfully describe model behavior. Unrestricted verification can exceed NP, so a practical NP solver would not settle every verification problem.

Roster comparison—CSC-07, Reliable machine-checked mathematical discovery: efficient search could help discover proofs when their lengths and checking costs fit a suitable polynomially verifiable formulation. It would not guarantee short proofs for arbitrary theorems or identify which mathematical questions are valuable. Reliable discovery also requires formalization and trustworthy checking. Conversely, machine-checked discovery could advance substantially without a general practical NP-complete solver.

Roster comparison—CSC-05, Routine-cost general computation on encrypted data, and CSC-09, Practical indistinguishability obfuscation: these seek useful computation while preserving computational secrecy, whereas CSC-01 would threaten the hardness assumptions on which their computational security depends. This is a conceptual consequence of general efficient search, not a claim that any supplied source evaluates those roster entries or their concrete attack costs. Their practicality problems and CSC-01's algorithmic objective remain distinct.

The cryptographic relationship is asymmetric: a practical constructive proof of P = NP would undermine computational hardness, but a proof of P ≠ NP alone would not establish one-way functions or public-key encryption. Worst-case difficulty does not by itself establish the average-case hardness needed for cryptography. The possible world called Pessiland combines hard NP problems with the absence of one-way functions. The supplied account comes from de Haan's lecture notes dated 12 March 2026 and the retained journal introduction, rather than a newly inspected copy of Impagliazzo's original 1995 paper.

Roster comparison—CSC-06, A predictive theory of generalization for modern learning systems: learning generalization concerns how performance transfers beyond observed training data. CSC-01 concerns correctness and computational cost across every input to an NP-complete problem. Better generalization theory could improve learning systems without resolving P versus NP; a practical NP solver would not by itself explain why a learned model generalizes.

brief.title: Practical ways to solve hard search problems
possible: People planning schedules, routes or designs could find exact solutions with a guaranteed limit on computing time, even for difficult cases. When no solution exists, the same method could establish that.

The target is a method that follows fixed rules and solves an NP-complete problem: one that can express every problem whose proposed solutions are quick to check. Its maximum running time would grow as a fixed power of input size, with costs low enough for practical use.
why: For planners, engineers and researchers, checking a proposed answer would become a route to finding one across a broad class of problems. Exact search would gain a general performance guarantee beyond the many cases that existing tools already solve.

It would also undermine conventional encryption whose security depends on computations being too expensive to perform. The consequences would reach both people protecting information and those trying to recover it.

sources.showed: Cook explains why an algorithm with a fixed-power time bound for an NP-complete problem would settle whether finding answers can be as efficient as checking them. He also distinguishes that bound from practical affordability.
sources.quote: (c) If L is NP-complete and L ∈ P, then P=NP.
sources.cited_for: Solving an NP-complete problem efficiently would extend efficient computation across all problems with efficiently checkable solutions.
sources.not_established: This establishes the mathematical connection, without providing the practical algorithm.

sources.showed: They derive functions that are harder to reverse than to compute under a strong assumption about difficulty on typical inputs. They also prove limits on certain approaches using weaker assumptions.
sources.quote: We provide heuristic support for this very strong average-case hardness notion by showing that it holds for a random language.
sources.cited_for: Difficulty on typical inputs and the existence of cryptographic building blocks have a more complicated relationship than worst-case difficulty alone.
sources.not_established: The results neither supply a practical general search algorithm nor prove that ordinary computational difficulty guarantees secure encryption.

The central question remains open: nobody has established the practical general method described here, or proved that such a method cannot exist.

A proof must bound the longest possible running time while keeping actual computing costs affordable.
An implementation must account for memory, translating applications into inputs and recovering solutions, with independent reproduction.

milestones.label: A correct algorithm with a practical worst-case bound
milestones.explanation: A fully specified algorithm following fixed rules would need a rigorous proof of correctness and a practical fixed-power time bound for an NP-complete problem. This would establish the core mathematical and practical capability.

milestones.label: Independent runs succeed where existing solvers exhaust resources
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would reproduce public tests across encryption, combinatorial and industrial problems, reporting failures and all computing costs. This would establish useful performance beyond existing solvers' resource limits.

milestones.label: Proofs establish generality and tests establish practical breadth
milestones.explanation: Proofs would establish correctness and running-time guarantees for every input, while tests would establish useful performance across tested families. Together they would distinguish the capability from a benchmark win.

uncertain: It remains unknown whether efficient general search is mathematically possible, and whether it could also be practical.
No agreed threshold defines an acceptable running-time bound, benchmark suite or computing budget.
The costs of translating applications, recovering solutions and attacking encryption would depend on the actual algorithm.

page.title: Deterministic polynomial-time SAT solving
page.definition: A deterministic algorithm decides whether a Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form has an assignment of true or false to its variables that makes every clause true. One fixed polynomial in the encoded formula length bounds its running time on every input. An implementation of that algorithm wins the SAT Competition main track. SAT is NP-complete: every decision problem whose yes answers have polynomial-length, polynomial-time-checkable certificates reduces to SAT in polynomial time.

goal.need: In the US broadcast spectrum auction, a station’s price froze if a solver ran out of time checking whether it could be assigned a channel without excessive interference. Missing one feasible assignment could cost the government millions of dollars. A specialized SAT solver answered over 96% of checks within a minute in simulations. A polynomial worst-case bound for SAT would extend to NP-complete scheduling and routing decisions too. Avoiding a missed price reduction would still depend on finishing within the bidding deadline.

statements.quote: If it is easy to check that a solution to a problem is correct, is it also easy to solve the problem?
statements.context: Clay presents P versus NP as a Millennium Prize Problem. Resolving the question can establish either equality or inequality; this capability requires a constructive equality result.

statements.quote: Promotion of SAT solvers and their development
statements.context: One of the competition’s explicitly listed goals.

statements.body: Clay Mathematics Institute, official problem description by Stephen Cook
statements.quote: Most complexity theorists believe that P ≠ NP.
statements.context: The Millennium Prize problem asks whether P equals NP. A proof that the classes differ would settle the prize problem and rule out a deterministic polynomial-time SAT algorithm.

completion.title: An implementation of a proved polynomial-time SAT algorithm wins the SAT Competition main track.
completion.criterion: One fully specified deterministic algorithm correctly decides every CNF-SAT input with a proved polynomial worst-case bound in encoded input length N. Its correctness and complexity proofs receive acceptance after peer review. An implementation covered by those proofs ranks first in an official SAT Competition main track under that edition’s published hardware, benchmark, timeout, memory and certificate-checking rules. The proof covers all executed procedures, including preprocessing and certificate production.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback combining the complexity community’s polynomial-time criterion with the SAT Competition organizers’ first-place criterion; neither body publishes this combined test.
completion.basis: Searches of Clay’s problem statement, the SAT handbook, and SAT Competition rules and results found no externally defined practical polynomial-time SAT threshold. This fallback pairs an accepted mathematical proof with an existing competitive evaluation. Competition success establishes performance on its finite benchmark set; it does not establish affordable worst-case computation at every input size.

milestones.title: A complete SAT solver terminates with the correct answer on every finite CNF formula.
milestones.criterion: A deterministic program halts on every finite formula in conjunctive normal form, an AND of clauses, each an OR of variables or their negations. It returns satisfiable exactly when some assignment makes every clause true and returns unsatisfiable otherwise.
milestones.set_by: SAT-solving community convention of sound and complete algorithms, stated by Darwiche and Pipatsrisawat in Complete Algorithms, section 3.1.
milestones.threshold_quote: algorithms that are guaranteed to terminate with a correct decision on the satisfiability/unsatisfiability of the given CNF.

milestones.title: A SAT solver achieves first place in the SAT Competition main track.
milestones.criterion: An eligible sequential solver ranks first in the official overall main-track standings across satisfiable and unsatisfiable instances under that edition’s scoring and certificate rules. In 2025, PAR-2 charged each unsolved instance twice the 5,000-second timeout, the solver memory limit was 30 GB, and the certificate-checking tool chain had 45,000 seconds.
milestones.set_by: SAT Competition organizing committee, published main-track rules and results.
milestones.threshold_quote: Solvers in all tracks will be ranked based on the PAR-2 score

milestones.title: A deterministic 3-SAT algorithm has a proved subexponential worst-case time bound.
milestones.criterion: One deterministic algorithm correctly decides every 3-SAT formula in worst-case time bounded by 2^{g(n)} times a polynomial in the encoded input length. Each clause contains at most three literals, n is the number of variables, and g(n)/n tends to zero as n tends to infinity.
milestones.set_by: Computational complexity community, through Impagliazzo and Paturi’s Exponential-Time Hypothesis in On the Complexity of k-SAT; this milestone refutes the hypothesis for 3-SAT.
milestones.threshold_quote: k-SAT does not have a subexponential-time algorithm.

milestones.title: A deterministic SAT algorithm has an accepted proof of polynomial worst-case running time.
milestones.criterion: An explicit deterministic Turing machine correctly decides every CNF-SAT input. For one fixed integer k and every encoded input length N, its worst-case number of steps T(N) satisfies T(N) ≤ N^k + k. Its correctness and running-time proofs receive acceptance after peer review.
milestones.set_by: Computational complexity community; Cook’s official Clay problem description, definition of P and Proposition 1(c).
milestones.threshold_quote: bounded by some fixed polynomial in the length of the input.

milestones.title: A deterministic 3-SAT algorithm attains the (4/3)^{n+o(n)} worst-case time bound.
milestones.criterion: One deterministic algorithm correctly decides every formula with at most three literals per clause in worst-case time bounded by (4/3)^{n+o(n)} times a polynomial in the encoded input length, where n is the number of variables.
milestones.set_by: Exact SAT algorithms community, through the deterministic form of Schöning’s bound in Moser and Scheder’s Theorem 5 and its use as a baseline by Liu.
milestones.threshold_quote: There is a deterministic algorithm solving \(k\)-SAT in time \(\left(\frac{2(k-1)}{k}\right)^{n+o(n)}\).

not_found: No outside body was found to define a combined polynomial-time proof and practical-performance completion test for NP-complete algorithms.
No externally prescribed milestone sequence connecting complete SAT solving, competition performance and polynomial-time proofs was located.
No peer-reviewed publication of the 27 October 2026 subexponential 3-SAT claim was located.

definition = "A deterministic algorithm decides whether a Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form has an assignment of true or false to its variables that makes every clause true. One fixed polynomial in the encoded formula length bounds its running time on every input. An implementation of that algorithm wins the SAT Competition main track. SAT is NP-complete: every decision problem whose yes answers have polynomial-length, polynomial-time-checkable certificates reduces to SAT in polynomial time.". Reason: The definition omits the polynomial length bound on NP certificates and leaves the size used to measure running time implicit.

goal.need = "In the US broadcast spectrum auction, a station\u2019s price froze if a solver ran out of time checking whether it could be assigned a channel without excessive interference. Missing one feasible assignment could cost the government millions of dollars. A specialized SAT solver answered over 96% of checks within a minute in simulations. A polynomial worst-case bound for SAT would extend to NP-complete scheduling and routing decisions too. Avoiding a missed price reduction would still depend on finishing within the bidding deadline.". Reason: The spectrum auction quantifies what an unresolved feasibility check can cost and shows when a better worst-case bound would benefit a user.
